claim: Cardiomyocyte (CM) maturation in mammals is accompanied by a sharp decline in their proliferative and regenerative potential shortly after birth.
source: Cardiomyocyte (CM) maturation in mammals is accompanied by a sharp decline in their proliferative and regenerative potential shortly after birth.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Rat and mouse neonatal CMs cultured on rigid surfaces exhibited increased myofibrillar organization, spread morphology, and reduced cell cycle activity.
source: We show that rat and mouse neonatal CMs cultured on rigid surfaces exhibited increased myofibrillar organization, spread morphology, and reduced cell cycle activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1, showing morphological and proliferation differences between rigid and compliant substrates.

claim: Compliant elastic matrices induced features of CM dedifferentiation, including a disorganized sarcomere network, rounding, and conspicuous cell-cycle re-entry.
source: In contrast, compliant elastic matrices induced features of CM dedifferentiation, including a disorganized sarcomere network, rounding, and conspicuous cell-cycle re-entry.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 3 showing sarcomere disorganization, cell rounding, and increased proliferation markers on compliant substrates.

claim: The rigid matrix facilitated nuclear division (karyokinesis) leading to binucleation.
source: The rigid matrix facilitated nuclear division (karyokinesis) leading to binucleation, while compliant matrices promoted CM mitotic rounding and cell division (cytokinesis), associated with loss of differentiation markers.
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data in Figure 2 showing karyokinesis without cytokinesis on rigid substrates.

claim: Compliant matrices promoted CM mitotic rounding and cell division (cytokinesis), associated with loss of differentiation markers.
source: The rigid matrix facilitated nuclear division (karyokinesis) leading to binucleation, while compliant matrices promoted CM mitotic rounding and cell division (cytokinesis), associated with loss of differentiation markers.
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data in Figure 2 and immunofluorescence data in Figure 3 showing complete cell division and loss of cTnT/MHC on compliant substrates.

claim: The compliant matrix potentiated clonal expansion of CMs that involves multiple cell divisions.
source: Moreover, the compliant matrix potentiated clonal expansion of CMs that involves multiple cell divisions.
evidence: This is supported by clonal tracing experiments using Myh6-Cre;R26R-Confetti-lox mice shown in Figure 5.

claim: During the early postnatal period, cardiomyocytes (CMs) undergo a switch from a proliferative, hyperplastic mode to non-proliferative, hypertrophic growth that persists throughout life.
source: During the early postnatal period, cardiomyocytes (CMs) undergo a switch from a proliferative, hyperplastic mode to non-proliferative, hypertrophic growth that persists throughout life (Li et al., 1996; Soonpaa et al., 1996; Soonpaa and Field, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The expression of cell-cycle and embryonic markers falls precipitously in CMs during postnatal maturation.
source: The expression of cell-cycle and embryonic markers falls precipitously in CMs (Walsh et al., 2010), while the expression of CM differentiation genes increases, along with the appearance of sarcomeres, contractile units that undergo cross-striation to form a functional myoskeletal system within CMs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walsh et al., 2010.

claim: Up-regulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components and increased cross-linking of matrix proteins occurs postnatally, leading to an overall stiffening of the heart tissue.
source: In parallel, up-regulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components, as well as increased cross-linking of matrix proteins, also occurs postnatally, leading to an overall stiffening of the heart tissue (Janmey and Miller, 2011; Swift et al., 2013; Majkut et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Over the first week of postnatal life in mice, most CMs exit the cell cycle and differentiate.
source: Over the first week of postnatal life in mice, most CMs exit the cell cycle and differentiate (Soonpaa et al., 1996), although some CMs undergo an additional burst of proliferation in the pre-adolescent period, driven by the thyroid hormone (Naqvi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soonpaa et al., 1996 and Naqvi et al., 2014.

claim: Mammalian CMs display a fetal/neonatal phase in which nuclear division (karyokinesis) is immediately followed by cell division (cytokinesis).
source: Mammalian CMs display distinct cycling phases: a fetal/neonatal phase in which nuclear division (karyokinesis) is immediately followed by cell division (cytokinesis), and a later neonatal phase, in which karyokinesis proceeds without cytokinesis, leading to binucleation (Soonpaa et al., 1996; Li et al., 1997a, 1997b; Zebrowski and Engel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mammalian CMs display a later neonatal phase in which karyokinesis proceeds without cytokinesis, leading to binucleation.
source: Mammalian CMs display distinct cycling phases: a fetal/neonatal phase in which nuclear division (karyokinesis) is immediately followed by cell division (cytokinesis), and a later neonatal phase, in which karyokinesis proceeds without cytokinesis, leading to binucleation (Soonpaa et al., 1996; Li et al., 1997a, 1997b; Zebrowski and Engel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Binucleation, hypertrophic growth, increased myofibrillar organization, and cell cycle withdrawal are all manifestations of the differentiated state of adult CMs.
source: Binucleation, hypertrophic growth, increased myofibrillar organization, and cell cycle withdrawal are all manifestations of the differentiated state of adult CMs (Ahuja et al., 2007; Naqvi et al., 2009; Zebrowski and Engel, 2013), while the 'terminal differentiation' state is yet uncertain.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Myocardial infarction (MI) is a life-threatening disease leading to permanent loss of hundreds of millions of CMs, followed by an inflammatory response and formation of scar tissue.
source: In humans, myocardial infarction (MI) is a life-threatening disease leading to permanent loss of hundreds of millions of CMs, followed by an inflammatory response and formation of scar tissue, that progressively lead to cardiac dysfunction and heart failure (Virag and Murry, 2003; Ausoni and Sartore, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The zebrafish heart is able to fully regenerate after injury, without scarring.
source: The zebrafish heart, for example, is able to fully regenerate after injury, without scarring (Poss et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Poss et al., 2002.

claim: The neonatal murine heart displays a transient regenerative phase that diminishes within the first week after birth.
source: The lack of regenerative potential of the mammalian heart was challenged by Porrello and colleagues (Porrello et al., 2011), who showed that the neonatal murine heart displays a transient regenerative phase that diminishes within the first week after birth.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Porrello et al., 2011.

claim: Both mammalian and zebrafish heart regeneration is characterized by increased CM proliferation associated with sarcomere disassembly, attributed to a CM dedifferentiation process.
source: Both mammalian and zebrafish heart regeneration is characterized by increased CM proliferation associated with sarcomere disassembly, attributed to a CM dedifferentiation process (Poss, 2007; Jopling et al., 2010, 2011; Porrello et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The rigidity of the underlying matrix strongly influences cell structure, cytoskeletal organization, migration, polarization, and regulation of gene expression and cell fate.
source: Recent studies with diverse cell types indicate that the rigidity of the underlying (or surrounding) matrix strongly influences cell structure, cytoskeletal organization, migration, polarization, and regulation of gene expression and cell fate (Pelham and Wang, 1997; Discher et al., 2005; Engler et al., 2006; Vogel and Sheetz, 2006; Engler et al., 2008; Geiger et al., 2009; Prager-Khoutorsky et al., 2011; Shin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Interaction with rigid surfaces (hundreds of kPa and stiffer) promotes the formation of large, integrin-mediated adhesions, and consequently, development of a well-organized and polarized cytoskeleton.
source: In particular, it was demonstrated that interaction with rigid surfaces (hundreds of kPa and stiffer) promotes the formation of large, integrin-mediated adhesions, and consequently, development of a well-organized and polarized cytoskeleton (Prager-Khoutorsky et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prager-Khoutorsky et al., 2011.

claim: CMs on the rigid substrate displayed aligned sarcomeres with defined and registered striations.
source: Myosin heavy chain (MHC), Myomesin (an M-band protein) and cardiac Troponin T (cTnT) were expressed in CMs cultured on both rigid and compliant substrates; however, CMs on the rigid substrate displayed aligned sarcomeres with defined and registered striations, whereas CMs on the compliant substrate had disorganized sarcomeres, with misaligned myoskeletal structures (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CMs on the compliant substrate had disorganized sarcomeres, with misaligned myoskeletal structures.
source: Myosin heavy chain (MHC), Myomesin (an M-band protein) and cardiac Troponin T (cTnT) were expressed in CMs cultured on both rigid and compliant substrates; however, CMs on the rigid substrate displayed aligned sarcomeres with defined and registered striations, whereas CMs on the compliant substrate had disorganized sarcomeres, with misaligned myoskeletal structures (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CMs cultured on the rigid substrate appeared larger, elongated, and mostly triangular.
source: Furthermore, CMs cultured on the rigid substrate appeared larger, elongated, and mostly triangular, whereas CMs on the compliant substrate were round, smaller, and less polarized.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: CMs on the compliant substrate were round, smaller, and less polarized.
source: Furthermore, CMs cultured on the rigid substrate appeared larger, elongated, and mostly triangular, whereas CMs on the compliant substrate were round, smaller, and less polarized.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: CM proliferation was increased on the compliant substrates (5 kPa and 20 kPa) by ∼50–65%, respectively, relative to the rigid substrate as visualized with Ki67.
source: However, CM proliferation was increased on the compliant substrates (5 kPa and 20 kPa) by ∼50–65%, respectively, relative to the rigid substrate (Figure 1G, visualized with Ki67), and by ∼25–110% on the 5 kPa and 20 kPa substrates, respectively, marked by PH3+ MHC+ CMs (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of Ki67+ cells shown in Figure 1G.

claim: CM proliferation was increased by ∼25–110% on the 5 kPa and 20 kPa substrates, respectively, marked by PH3+ MHC+ CMs.
source: However, CM proliferation was increased on the compliant substrates (5 kPa and 20 kPa) by ∼50–65%, respectively, relative to the rigid substrate (Figure 1G, visualized with Ki67), and by ∼25–110% on the 5 kPa and 20 kPa substrates, respectively, marked by PH3+ MHC+ CMs (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of PH3+ MHC+ cells shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Both the 5 kPa and 20 kPa substrates facilitated mouse CM proliferation by ∼30–50%, respectively, relative to the rigid 2 MPa substrate.
source: We quantified the percentage of proliferating Ki67+ cTnT+ CMs, and observed that both the 5 kPa and 20 kPa substrates facilitated CM proliferation by ∼30–50%, respectively, relative to the rigid 2 MPa substrate (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1I,J.

claim: Live-cell video microscopy revealed two distinct CM cell-cycle phenotypes: karyokinesis followed by binucleation, as opposed to karyokinesis followed by cytokinesis, resulting in the formation of two new CMs.
source: Live-cell video microscopy revealed two distinct CM cell-cycle phenotypes: karyokinesis followed by binucleation (Figure 2C, Video 1), as opposed to karyokinesis followed by cytokinesis, resulting in the formation of two new CMs (Figure 2D, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2C, 2D and Videos 1, 2.

claim: Compliant matrices did not affect nuclear cell division (karyokinesis), yet promoted cytokinesis and inhibited CM binucleation prominence.
source: Strikingly, we found that compliant matrices did not affect nuclear cell division (karyokinesis), yet promoted cytokinesis and inhibited CM binucleation prominence, as determined by quantification of the division frequency, observed by live-cell imaging (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of karyokinesis, cytokinesis, and binucleation events shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: A significant increase in the number of newly formed CMs was observed on the 20 kPa substrate, relative to the rigid 2 MPa.
source: In order to demonstrate an actual increase in CM number, we quantified the amount of CMs at the beginning and after 48 hr. A significant increase in the number of newly formed CMs was observed on the 20 kPa substrate, relative to the rigid 2 MPa (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Culturing CMs on compliant matrices facilitate CM cell rounding and division (cytokinesis) that lead to formation of new CMs.
source: Taken together, our findings demonstrate that culturing CMs on compliant matrices facilitate CM cell rounding and division (cytokinesis) that lead to formation of new CMs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the live-cell imaging data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The rigid matrix promotes karyokinesis without cytokinesis, leading to CM binucleation.
source: In contrast, our results demonstrated that the rigid matrix promotes karyokinesis without cytokinesis, leading to CM binucleation (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Under regular conditions, almost 100% of dTomato+/cTnT+ double positive CMs were detected.
source: Under regular conditions, we detected almost 100% of dTomato+/cTnT+ double positive CMs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dividing CMs (tdTomato positive) lost cTnT expression, either completely or partially.
source: By correlating the last frame of each time-lapse video (Figure 3A–C) with cTnT staining, we revealed that the dividing CMs (tdTomato positive; Figure 3A′,B′,C′) lost cTnT expression, either completely (Figure 3A′′,B′′), or partially (Figure 3C′′).
evidence: This is supported by correlative live-cell immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: The majority of dividing CMs expressed Ki67 on all three matrices, indicating that these CMs maintain a proliferative potential.
source: Furthermore, the majority of these cells expressed Ki67 on all three matrices, indicating that these CMs maintain a proliferative potential (Figure 3A′′′,B′′′,C′′′).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A''', B''', C'''.

claim: A ∼twofold increase in CM dedifferentiation (Tomato+/cTnT− and Tomato+/MHC−) was observed on the 20 kPa, and an ∼1.5-fold increase, on the 5 kPa matrices, relative to the rigid matrix.
source: A ∼twofold increase in CM dedifferentiation (Tomato+/cTnT− and Tomato+/MHC−) was observed on the 20 kPa, and an ∼1.5-fold increase, on the 5 kPa matrices, relative to the rigid matrix (Figure 3E,G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3E and 3G.

claim: All Myh6 lineage-positive (tdTomato+) CMs in the culture expressed Nkx2.5, indicating that these cells derived from the cardiac lineage.
source: Moreover, all Myh6 lineage-positive (tdTomato+) CMs in the culture expressed Nkx2.5, indicating that these cells derived from the cardiac lineage (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Blebbistatin severely disrupted CM myoskeleton morphology, leading to massive changes in CM cell shape, manifested by major flattening, dramatic fragmentation of the sarcomeric arrays, and complete loss of striations.
source: We found that blebbistatin severely disrupted CM myoskeleton morphology, leading to massive changes in CM cell shape, manifested by major flattening, dramatic fragmentation of the sarcomeric arrays, and complete loss of striations (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Blebbistatin-treated CMs display higher cell cycle activity compared to control (untreated) CMs on the 2 MPa and 20 kPa rigidities.
source: This analysis indicated that blebbistatin-treated CMs display higher cell cycle activity compared to control (untreated) CMs on the 2 MPa and 20 kPa rigidities (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of Ki67+ cells shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Relaxation of the acto-myosin myoskelton in CMs by blebbistatin promotes cell cycle re-entry.
source: Hence, we conclude that relaxation of the acto-myosin myoskelton in CMs by blebbistatin promotes cell cycle re-entry.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the blebbistatin treatment data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Complaint matrices promote CM proliferation primarily via their effect on myoskeletal organization.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that complaint matrices promote CM proliferation primarily via their effect on myoskeletal organization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the blebbistatin treatment data and the observation that blebbistatin had no effect on the 5 kPa substrate.

claim: The 20 kPa substrate facilitates a 2.4-fold increase in CM number, relative to 2 MPa.
source: We found ∼2.4-fold higher numbers of total CMs formed on the 20 kPa relative to the 2 MPa substrate (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data from clonal tracing experiments shown in Figure 5G.

claim: A ∼twofold increase in the percentage of unicolor clones was observed on the 20 kPa substrate, compared to both the rigid 2 MPa and softest 5 kPa substrates.
source: A ∼twofold increase in the percentage of unicolor clones was observed on the 20 kPa substrate, compared to both the rigid 2 MPa and softest 5 kPa substrates (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data from clonal tracing experiments shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The 20 kPa matrix induced an impressive increase in CM cell number over time.
source: Next, we quantified the number of cells in all the clones, at each time point, and found that the 20 kPa matrix induced an impressive increase in CM cell number (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data from clonal tracing experiments shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Neonatal CMs can undergo clonal expansion in vitro, a process which involves multiple cell divisions.
source: This analysis revealed that neonatal CMs can undergo clonal expansion in vitro, a process which involves multiple cell divisions; moreover, this potential can be induced most readily on the 20 kPa matrix, compared to either rigid or softer matrices.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the clonal tracing data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Neonatal CMs cultured on compliant (compared to rigid) 2D matrices lose several key manifestations commonly associated with postnatal cardiac muscle differentiation in vivo.
source: Here, we show that neonatal CMs cultured on compliant (compared to rigid) 2D matrices lose several key manifestations commonly associated with postnatal cardiac muscle differentiation in vivo, such as robust, well-aligned myoskeletel organization, expression of differentiation genes, and cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Compliant substrates promote CM dedifferentiation and proliferation.
source: Hence, we conclude that compliant substrates promote CM dedifferentiation and proliferation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the study, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Dedifferentiated CMs were able to undergo clonal expansion, which involves multiple cell divisions, suggesting a shift to a progenitor cell state.
source: In line with these findings, we demonstrated that dedifferentiated CMs were able to undergo clonal expansion, which involves multiple cell divisions, suggesting a shift to a progenitor cell state.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the clonal tracing data shown in Figure 5 and the dedifferentiation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The rigidification of the heart after birth from 10-20 kPa to 40–55 kPa promotes CM terminal differentiation by triggering the formation of a rigid myoskeleton that mechanically interferes with CM cytokinesis, without affecting karyokinesis.
source: We propose that the rigidification of the heart after birth from 10-20 kPa to 40–55 kPa (Berry et al., 2006; Engler et al., 2008; Jacot et al., 2010) promotes CM terminal differentiation by triggering the formation of a rigid myoskeleton that mechanically interferes with CM cytokinesis, without affecting karyokinesis.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data and cited literature on heart stiffness changes.

claim: CM shape is linked to sarcomeric alignment; circular CMs do not assemble actin networks or sarcomeric arrays, whereas rectangular CMs do.
source: It was previously shown that CM shape is linked to sarcomeric alignment (Bray et al., 2008); circular CMs do not assemble actin networks or sarcomeric arrays, whereas rectangular CMs do.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bray et al., 2008.

claim: Eukaryotic cell division requires cellular and cytoskeletal remodeling: cells become round and spherical upon entering mitosis.
source: Eukaryotic cell division requires cellular and cytoskeletal remodeling: cells become round and spherical upon entering mitosis (Heng and Koh, 2010; Lancaster et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mitotic rounding is considered a hallmark of cell division.
source: This mitotic rounding is, to some extent, considered a hallmark of cell division, and the interplay between the actin cytoskeleton, cell shape, and the developing mitotic spindle are all involved in this rounding (Cadart et al., 2014; Lancaster and Baum, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cytoskeletal organization and cell-cycle control are linked together.
source: Thus, it appears that cytoskeletal organization and cell-cycle control are linked together.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature cited and the experimental data presented.

claim: Inhibition of the organized CM contractile apparatus following blebbistatin treatment resulted in increased CM cell cycle re-entry.
source: In line with this notion, we demonstrate that inhibition of the organized CM contractile apparatus following blebbistatin treatment resulted in increased CM cell cycle re-entry.
evidence: This is supported by the blebbistatin treatment data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The development of a robust myoskeleton in CMs is linked to their cell cycle arrest.
source: We show an increase in Ki67-expressing CMs in the presence of blebbistatin on the 2 MPa and 20 kPa rigidities. Blebbistatin treatment strongly perturbed CM myoskeletal organization and consequently induced CM cell cycle activity, suggesting that the development of a robust myoskeleton in CMs is linked to their cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the blebbistatin treatment data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The rigid matrix increases the forces imposed on the CMs' actin myoskeleton and this facilitates CM differentiation.
source: More broadly, we propose that the rigid matrix increases the forces imposed on the CMs' actin myoskeleton and this facilitates CM differentiation, while inhibition of sarcomeric organization, function and contractility by blebbistatin has the opposite effect, eventually, leading to CM dedifferentiation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data.

claim: Long blebbistatin treatment inhibits cell division, leading to generation of polyploid megakaryocytes.
source: That said, it was previously shown that long blebbistatin treatment inhibits cell division, leading to generation of polyploid megakaryocytes (Shin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shin et al., 2011.

claim: Polyploidity and binucleation are natural outcomes of postnatal CM proliferation events.
source: Polyploidity and binucleation are natural outcomes of postnatal CM proliferation events (Zebrowski and Engel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zebrowski and Engel, 2013.

claim: Cytokinesis, but not karyokinesis, is affected by matrix rigidity: it is facilitated by the compliant substrates, or inhibited by the rigid substrate.
source: One of the most important findings in this study is that cytokinesis, but not karyokinesis, is affected by matrix rigidity: it is facilitated by the compliant substrates, or inhibited by the rigid substrate.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Committed CMs cultured on the 20 kPa (and, to some extent, the 5 kPa) substrate lose the environmental mechanical barrier, leading to the disorganization of the myoskeleton, which facilitates the acquisition of a rounded morphology compatible with cytokinesis and cell division.
source: Taken together, the data presented here suggest that committed CMs cultured on the 20 kPa (and, to some extent, the 5 kPa) substrate lose the environmental mechanical barrier, leading to the disorganization of the myoskeleton, which facilitates the acquisition of a rounded morphology compatible with cytokinesis and cell division (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Transgenic expression of a constitutively active (ca) form of ErbB2 in mouse CMs during the neonatal and adult periods could stimulate CM division, expanding the postnatal proliferative and regenerative windows into adulthood.
source: Interestingly, transgenic expression of a constitutively active (ca) form of ErbB2 in mouse CMs during the neonatal and adult periods could stimulate CM division, expanding the postnatal proliferative and regenerative windows into adulthood. Stimulation of CM division by caErbB2 involved both CM dedifferentiation, and hypertrophy leading to cardiomegaly. In line with the observed dedifferentiation phenotype, caErbB2 signaling promoted proliferation of mono- and bi-nucleated CMs (D'Uva et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to D'Uva et al., 2015.

claim: Mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and MCF10A cells proliferate best on ∼24 kPa.
source: In line with our data, mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and MCF10A cells proliferate best on ∼24 kPa (Klein et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Klein et al., 2009.

claim: Muscle stem cells (MuSCs) that were cultured on a soft substrate that mimics muscle tissue rigidity (∼12 kPa) display delayed differentiation, self-renewal, and maintained stemness.
source: Moreover, muscle stem cells (MuSCs) that were cultured on a soft substrate that mimics muscle tissue rigidity (∼12 kPa) display delayed differentiation, self-renewal, and maintained stemness (Gilbert et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gilbert et al., 2010.

claim: Decreased rigidity preserves stemness by altering cell shape, resulting in cytoskeletal rearrangements.
source: In agreement with our findings, these researchers propose that decreased rigidity preserves stemness by altering cell shape, resulting in cytoskeletal rearrangements.
evidence: This is a conclusion from cited literature (Gilbert et al., 2010) that aligns with the current study's findings.

claim: In both neonatal mice and adult zebrafish, cardiac regeneration processes were accompanied by loss of sarcomeric structures and re-acquisition of cell division, both attributed to CM dedifferentiation.
source: In both neonatal mice and adult zebrafish, cardiac regeneration processes were accompanied by loss of sarcomeric structures and re-acquisition of cell division, both attributed to CM dedifferentiation (Poss, 2007; Jopling et al., 2010; Porrello et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Correlative live-imaging and immunostaining results support the notion that dedifferentiated CMs disassemble their sarcomeres, in order to divide.
source: Our correlative live-imaging and immunostaining results support the notion that dedifferentiated CMs disassemble their sarcomeres, in order to divide.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlative live-cell immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The fact that CMs have lost MHC or cTnT expression, and the partial disassembly of the sarcomeres during cytokinesis, further support the model of CM dedifferentiation, rather than the presence of progenitor cells.
source: The fact that CMs have lost MHC or cTnT expression, and the partial disassembly of the sarcomeres during cytokinesis, further support our model of CM dedifferentiation, rather than the presence of progenitor cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dedifferentiation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Clone formation originated at various time points and progressed at different rates, suggesting a continuous proliferative capacity, rather than a final 'burst' of proliferation.
source: We show that clonal expansion is rigidity-dependent, with an optimal clonal efficiency on the 20 kPa. Clone formation originated at various time points and progressed at different rates, suggesting a continuous proliferative capacity, rather than a final 'burst' of proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the clonal tracing data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the event of cardiac injury, CMs in the vicinity of the scar tissue sense a stiffer environment, compared to the healthy adult heart.
source: Our findings bear obvious relevance for cardiac regeneration after injury. In this unfortunate event, CMs in the vicinity of the scar tissue sense a stiffer environment, compared to the healthy adult heart (Jacot et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jacot et al., 2010.

claim: If fully differentiated CMs present in the vicinity of the damaged area can still maintain the capacity to dedifferentiate and resume cell division if confronted with a sufficiently compliant scaffold, a new avenue toward the regeneration of heart tissue may be opened.
source: Thus, if fully differentiated CMs present in the vicinity of the damaged area, can still maintain the capacity to dedifferentiate and resume cell division if confronted with a sufficiently compliant scaffold, a new avenue toward the regeneration of heart tissue may be opened.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications based on the study's findings.

claim: Neonatal rat CMs were isolated using RDB, a proteolytic enzyme extracted from the fig tree.
source: To obtain a CM-rich culture, the hearts were digested in RDB, a proteolytic enzyme extracted from the fig tree (Biological Institute, Nes Ziona, Israel) in 6–8 cycles of 10 min each, at room temperature.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: CMs began to beat spontaneously within 2–3 days on all of the tested substrates.
source: CMs began to beat spontaneously within 2–3 days, on all of the tested substrates.
evidence: This is an observation from the cell culture experiments.

claim: PDMS substrates with elastomer to curing agent ratios of 10:1, 50:1 and 75:1 corresponded to Young's moduli of 2 MPa, 20 kPa and 5 kPa, respectively.
source: Elastomer to curing agent ratios of 10:1, 50:1 and 75:1 corresponded to Young's moduli of 2 MPa, 20 kPa and 5 kPa, respectively.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section describing substrate preparation.

claim: The compliant microenvironment facilitates CM dedifferentiation and proliferation via its effect on the organization of the myoskeleton.
source: Thus, the compliant microenvironment facilitates CM dedifferentiation and proliferation via its effect on the organization of the myoskeleton.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the abstract based on all experimental data.

claim: CMs cultured on either glass or on the stiff (2 MPa) substrate presented similar proliferative capacities.
source: CMs cultured on either glass or on the stiff (2 MPa) substrate presented similar proliferative capacities (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation, though the data is not shown.

claim: CMs that completed cell division (cytokinesis) underwent a step of mitotic rounding.
source: In contrast, CMs that completed cell division (cytokinesis) underwent a step of mitotic rounding (Figure 2D), which is common for most proliferating cells (Lancaster and Baum, 2014); moreover, these CMs often underwent consecutive cell divisions.
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2D and citation to Lancaster and Baum, 2014.

claim: CMs that completed cytokinesis often underwent consecutive cell divisions.
source: In contrast, CMs that completed cell division (cytokinesis) underwent a step of mitotic rounding (Figure 2D), which is common for most proliferating cells (Lancaster and Baum, 2014); moreover, these CMs often underwent consecutive cell divisions.
evidence: This is an observation from live-cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 2D and Video 2.

claim: Rare events of cytokinesis were observed in binucleated CMs cultured on the 20 kPa substrate, resulting in two daughter CMs.
source: Interestingly, we could observe rare events of cytokinesis even in binucleated CMs cultured on the 20 kPa substrate, resulting in two daughter CMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Successful cytokinesis events in binucleated CMs were accompanied by mitotic rounding.
source: These successful events were also accompanied by mitotic rounding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lack of blebbistatin effect on the 5 kPa substrate is consistent with the relaxed CM morphology induced by the 5 kPa substrate in the absence of blebbistatin.
source: The lack of blebbistatin effect on the 5 kPa substrate is consistent with the relaxed CM morphology induced by the 5 kPa substrate in the absence of blebbistatin.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the blebbistatin treatment data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The high CM cell-cycle activity observed in the presence of blebbistatin may ultimately result in inhibition of cytokinesis, leading to CM binucleation, or even multinucleation.
source: It is possible that the high CM cell-cycle activity observed in the presence of blebbistatin may ultimately result in inhibition of cytokinesis, leading to CM binucleation, or even multinucleation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the blebbistatin data and cited literature.

claim: A proliferative burst on P15, induced by a thyroid hormone surge, led to a 1.4-fold increase in CM number.
source: Recently, the view that binucleated CMs cannot divide was challenged, showing that a proliferative burst on P15, induced by a thyroid hormone surge, led to a 1.4-fold increase in CM number (Naqvi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Naqvi et al., 2014.

claim: Most binucleated CMs attempting to divide remain binucleated.
source: We observed rare events of binucleated CMs attempting to divide, though most remain binucleated.
evidence: This is an observation from live-cell imaging experiments.

claim: The few successful division events of binucleated CMs were facilitated by growth on the 20 kPa matrix.
source: However, the few successful division events were facilitated by growth on the 20 kPa matrix, further supporting the notion that CM can respond to matrix rigidity.
evidence: This is an observation from live-cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: CMs can respond to matrix rigidity.
source: However, the few successful division events were facilitated by growth on the 20 kPa matrix, further supporting the notion that CM can respond to matrix rigidity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that binucleated CM division was facilitated on 20 kPa substrate.

claim: CaErbB2 signaling promoted proliferation of mono- and bi-nucleated CMs.
source: In line with the observed dedifferentiation phenotype, caErbB2 signaling promoted proliferation of mono- and bi-nucleated CMs (D'Uva et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to D'Uva et al., 2015.

claim: Stimulation of CM division by caErbB2 involved both CM dedifferentiation, and hypertrophy leading to cardiomegaly.
source: Stimulation of CM division by caErbB2 involved both CM dedifferentiation, and hypertrophy leading to cardiomegaly.
evidence: This is supported by citation to D'Uva et al., 2015.

claim: The mechanisms whereby complex developmental processes of CM maturation are regulated and coordinated, and their putative effects on CM maturation, are yet enigmatic.
source: The mechanisms whereby these complex developmental processes are regulated and coordinated, and their putative effects on CM maturation, are yet enigmatic.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The 'terminal differentiation' state of CMs is yet uncertain.
source: Binucleation, hypertrophic growth, increased myofibrillar organization, and cell cycle withdrawal are all manifestations of the differentiated state of adult CMs (Ahuja et al., 2007; Naqvi et al., 2009; Zebrowski and Engel, 2013), while the 'terminal differentiation' state is yet uncertain.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Loss of the proliferative potential of differentiated CMs creates a major barrier to cardiac regeneration after injury.
source: Naturally, there are physiological advantages in the postnatal maturation of CMs. Nonetheless, loss of the proliferative potential of differentiated CMs creates a major barrier to cardiac regeneration after injury.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Myocardial infarction progressively leads to cardiac dysfunction and heart failure.
source: In humans, myocardial infarction (MI) is a life-threatening disease leading to permanent loss of hundreds of millions of CMs, followed by an inflammatory response and formation of scar tissue, that progressively lead to cardiac dysfunction and heart failure (Virag and Murry, 2003; Ausoni and Sartore, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations and is established medical knowledge.

claim: Mechanical and electrical cell-to-cell communication between CMs is established via intercalated discs, containing gap junctions, adherens junctions and desmosomes.
source: Further, mechanical and electrical cell-to-cell communication between CMs is established via intercalated discs, containing gap junctions, adherens junctions and desmosomes (Noorman et al., 2009; Sheikh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some CMs undergo an additional burst of proliferation in the pre-adolescent period, driven by the thyroid hormone.
source: Over the first week of postnatal life in mice, most CMs exit the cell cycle and differentiate (Soonpaa et al., 1996), although some CMs undergo an additional burst of proliferation in the pre-adolescent period, driven by the thyroid hormone (Naqvi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Naqvi et al., 2014.

claim: The expression of CM differentiation genes increases during postnatal maturation, along with the appearance of sarcomeres.
source: The expression of cell-cycle and embryonic markers falls precipitously in CMs (Walsh et al., 2010), while the expression of CM differentiation genes increases, along with the appearance of sarcomeres, contractile units that undergo cross-striation to form a functional myoskeletal system within CMs.
evidence: This is a statement about CM maturation supported by citation.

claim: Sarcomeres are contractile units that undergo cross-striation to form a functional myoskeletal system within CMs.
source: The expression of cell-cycle and embryonic markers falls precipitously in CMs (Walsh et al., 2010), while the expression of CM differentiation genes increases, along with the appearance of sarcomeres, contractile units that undergo cross-striation to form a functional myoskeletal system within CMs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sarcomere structure and function.

claim: Myosin heavy chain (MHC), Myomesin (an M-band protein) and cardiac Troponin T (cTnT) were expressed in CMs cultured on both rigid and compliant substrates.
source: Myosin heavy chain (MHC), Myomesin (an M-band protein) and cardiac Troponin T (cTnT) were expressed in CMs cultured on both rigid and compliant substrates; however, CMs on the rigid substrate displayed aligned sarcomeres with defined and registered striations, whereas CMs on the compliant substrate had disorganized sarcomeres, with misaligned myoskeletal structures (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CMs cultured on the 20 kPa substrate had intermediate parameters in terms of their polarization and spreading morphologies, compared to the 2 MPa and the 5 kPa substrates.
source: CMs cultured on the 20 kPa substrate had intermediate parameters in terms of their polarization and spreading morphologies, compared to the 2 MPa and the 5 kPa substrates (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Proliferating CMs were observed on all tested matrices (Ki67+/cTnT+, and PH3+/MHC+).
source: Proliferating CMs were observed on all tested matrices (Ki67+/cTnT+, and PH3+/MHC+) (Figure 1E,F, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Myoskeletal disassembly, a tendency toward cell rounding, and increased CM proliferation are more compatible with compliant matrices, in comparison with the rigid matrix.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that myoskeletal disassembly, a tendency toward cell rounding, and increased CM proliferation are more compatible with compliant matrices, in comparison with the rigid matrix.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Mouse neonatal CMs grew on all substrates, and developed normal beating within 48–72 hr after seeding.
source: As in rat CMs, mouse neonatal CMs grew on all substrates, and developed normal beating within 48–72 hr after seeding.
evidence: This is an observation from cell culture experiments.

claim: Similar to the rat system, CMs cultured on the rigid substrate were elongated and more polarized, compared to those on the compliant substrates.
source: Similar to the rat system, CMs cultured on the rigid substrate were elongated and more polarized, compared to those on the compliant substrates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A decrease in CM cell perimeter, indicative of roundness, was observed on the compliant substrates, compared to the rigid one.
source: A decrease in CM cell perimeter, indicative of roundness, was observed on the compliant substrates, compared to the rigid one (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Compliant substrates promote CM proliferation as well as alterations in CM cell shape, in both rat and mouse neonatal cultures.
source: Hence, compliant substrates promote CM proliferation as well as alterations in CM cell shape, in both rat and mouse neonatal cultures.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 1 for both rat and mouse CMs.

claim: Various proliferation markers (e.g., Ki67, BrdU, PH3, and Aurora B) are widely used for cell-cycle assessment and quantification of cell proliferation.
source: Various proliferation markers (e.g., Ki67 shown in Figure 2A, BrdU, PH3, and Aurora B), are widely used for cell-cycle assessment and quantification of cell proliferation; however, they sometimes prove insufficient, especially in CMs in which polyploidization and binucleation are natural outcomes of cell proliferation in the postnatal period (Bersell et al., 2009; Zebrowski and Engel, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about common research methods, supported by citations.

claim: Proliferation markers sometimes prove insufficient for CMs in which polyploidization and binucleation are natural outcomes of cell proliferation in the postnatal period.
source: Various proliferation markers (e.g., Ki67 shown in Figure 2A, BrdU, PH3, and Aurora B), are widely used for cell-cycle assessment and quantification of cell proliferation; however, they sometimes prove insufficient, especially in CMs in which polyploidization and binucleation are natural outcomes of cell proliferation in the postnatal period (Bersell et al., 2009; Zebrowski and Engel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CMs undergoing karyokinesis followed by binucleation were relatively large, spread, and immotile.
source: In the first, CMs were relatively large, spread, and immotile (Figure 2C: 50′, 60′). These CMs underwent karyokinesis, leading to the formation of binucleated CMs (Figure 2C: 50′, 60′), while remaining well spread and attached to the substrate (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CMs undergoing karyokinesis leading to binucleation remained well spread and attached to the substrate.
source: These CMs underwent karyokinesis, leading to the formation of binucleated CMs (Figure 2C: 50′, 60′), while remaining well spread and attached to the substrate (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mitotic rounding is common for most proliferating cells.
source: In contrast, CMs that completed cell division (cytokinesis) underwent a step of mitotic rounding (Figure 2D), which is common for most proliferating cells (Lancaster and Baum, 2014); moreover, these CMs often underwent consecutive cell divisions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lancaster and Baum, 2014.

claim: There was no significant difference in the area of mouse CMs plated on the different substrates.
source: There was no significant difference in the area of cells plated on the different substrates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The newly formed CMs following cytokinesis are still connected, and both nuclei are Ki67+.
source: Immunofluorescent images of dividing neonatal CMs in culture. The newly formed CMs are still connected, and both nuclei are Ki67+ (red).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A with immunofluorescence imaging.

claim: The Myh6-Cre;R26R-tdTomato-lox system enables visualization and tracking of CMs that express or previously expressed the Myh6 gene.
source: The 'Tomato' cells represent CMs that express, or previously expressed, the Myh6 gene, a signature of CM differentiation.
evidence: This is based on the genetic lineage tracing system described in the methods.

claim: Myh6 is a signature gene of CM differentiation.
source: The 'Tomato' cells represent CMs that express, or previously expressed, the Myh6 gene, a signature of CM differentiation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Myh6 gene.

claim: Dividing CMs that lost cTnT expression is consistent with a CM dedifferentiation process.
source: This result is consistent with a CM dedifferentiation process, in which CMs, originating from the Myh6 lineage, lost cTnT expression (Figure 3A′′,B′′,C′′).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlative live-cell immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Compliant matrices promote the dedifferentiation of CMs, consistent with their role in promoting cytokinesis.
source: Our findings, showing dividing CMs that downregulated cTnT and/or MHC sarcomeric proteins and express Nkx2.5, strongly suggest that the compliant matrices promote the dedifferentiation of CMs, consistent with their role in promoting cytokinesis (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the dedifferentiation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Blebbistatin is a small molecule myosin II inhibitor that effectively blocks the actin-myosin interaction in several striated muscle (including CMs), in smooth muscle, and in non-muscle cells.
source: For that purpose, we used blebbistatin, a small molecule myosin II inhibitor that effectively blocks the actin-myosin interaction in several striated muscle (including CMs), in smooth muscle, and in non-muscle cells (Dou et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dou et al., 2007.

claim: Disruption of the CM myoskeleton promotes CM cell cycle re-entry.
source: Our findings thus far suggest that disruption of the CM myoskeleton promotes CM cell cycle re-entry.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the blebbistatin treatment data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Inhibition of the CM myoskeleton function could boost CM proliferation.
source: We therefore tested whether inhibition of the CM myoskeleton function could boost CM proliferation.
evidence: This is the hypothesis tested with blebbistatin treatment.

claim: Neonatal mouse CMs were cultured on PDMS substrates with different rigidities, left to adhere for 72 hr, and then treated with 20 µM blebbistatin for 24 hr.
source: Neonatal mouse CMs were cultured on PDMS substrates with the different rigidities, left to adhere for 72 hr, and then treated with 20 µM blebbistatin for 24 hr.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedure.

claim: A closer examination of CMs derived from the Myh6 lineage that were grown on the 20 kPa matrix and lost cTnT and/or MHC expression, revealed clusters of cells (more than 2), suggesting that these cells were derived from a common CM that underwent multiple cell divisions.
source: A closer examination of CMs derived from the Myh6 lineage that were grown on the 20 kPa matrix and lost cTnT and/or MHC expression, revealed clusters of cells (more than 2), suggesting that these cells were derived from a common CM that underwent multiple cell divisions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The R26R-Confetti reporter line generates stochastic, multicolor Myh6 lineage-derived CMs with four fluorescent proteins, each marking individual clones.
source: To explore this notion further, we took advantage of the R26R-Confetti reporter line (Snippert et al., 2010). In this setting, the R26R-Confetti reporter generated stochastic, multicolor Myh6 lineage-derived CMs with four fluorescent proteins, each marking individual clones (Figure 5A–F; high magnification areas showing heterogeneous multicolor CM clones in vivo D, E, or individual YFP+ CM clones in F).
evidence: This is a description of the genetic tool used, supported by citation to Snippert et al., 2010.

claim: Unicolor clones, likely originating from a single CM, were identified on all three rigidities.
source: Unicolor clones, likely originating from a single CM, were identified on all three rigidities.
evidence: This is an observation from the clonal tracing experiments.

claim: A typical clonal expansion of an individual YFP-positive clone expanded from only 2 cells at Day 4, to 9 cells within a week (Day 11).
source: A typical clonal expansion of an individual YFP-positive clone, from only 2 cells at Day 4, to 9 cells within a week (Day 11), is shown (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The clonal expansion potential of neonatal CMs can be induced most readily on the 20 kPa matrix, compared to either rigid or softer matrices.
source: This analysis revealed that neonatal CMs can undergo clonal expansion in vitro, a process which involves multiple cell divisions; moreover, this potential can be induced most readily on the 20 kPa matrix, compared to either rigid or softer matrices.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the clonal tracing data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Most studies that address the impact of rigidity on cell fate decisions have focused on the differentiation processes.
source: Notably, most studies that address the impact of rigidity on cell fate decisions have focused on the differentiation processes (Engler et al., 2008; Jacot et al., 2008; Bajaj et al., 2010; Bhana et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The terminology and characteristics of the dedifferentiation process are much less clear than differentiation, but generally refer to the shift from a differentiated to a less-differentiated cellular stage within the same lineage.
source: The terminology and characteristics of the reverse process are much less clear, but generally refer to the shift from a differentiated to a less-differentiated cellular stage within the same lineage (Jopling et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the literature, supported by citation to Jopling et al., 2011.

claim: The heart rigidifies after birth from 10-20 kPa to 40–55 kPa.
source: We propose that the rigidification of the heart after birth from 10-20 kPa to 40–55 kPa (Berry et al., 2006; Engler et al., 2008; Jacot et al., 2010) promotes CM terminal differentiation by triggering the formation of a rigid myoskeleton that mechanically interferes with CM cytokinesis, without affecting karyokinesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berry et al., 2006; Engler et al., 2008; Jacot et al., 2010.

claim: The physiological transition of heart rigidification leads to an accumulation of binucleated CMs, correlating with the transition from embryonic hyperplastic growth of CMs, to postnatal hypertrophic growth.
source: Ultimately, this physiological transition leads to an accumulation of binucleated CMs, correlating with the transition from embryonic hyperplastic growth of CMs, to postnatal hypertrophic growth (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: The interplay between the actin cytoskeleton, cell shape, and the developing mitotic spindle are all involved in mitotic rounding.
source: This mitotic rounding is, to some extent, considered a hallmark of cell division, and the interplay between the actin cytoskeleton, cell shape, and the developing mitotic spindle are all involved in this rounding (Cadart et al., 2014; Lancaster and Baum, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mechanisms underlying CM binucleation, due to failure to complete cytokinesis, are poorly understood.
source: The mechanisms underlying CM binucleation, due to failure to complete cytokinesis, are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The view that binucleated CMs cannot divide was recently challenged.
source: Recently, the view that binucleated CMs cannot divide was challenged, showing that a proliferative burst on P15, induced by a thyroid hormone surge, led to a 1.4-fold increase in CM number (Naqvi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Naqvi et al., 2014.

claim: Whether neonatal or adult CMs are capable of undergoing multiple cycles of cell division in vivo, has yet to be determined.
source: Whether neonatal or adult CMs are capable of undergoing multiple cycles of cell division in vivo, has yet to be determined.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge and future research directions.
